inline.s: Alas! People today are forever saying that a woman’s disposition is as changeable as water, and so it is hard to achieve an immediate and perfect effect in instructing her; a claim like this is truly without reason! Now that a woman is born, if her parents have already failed in the way they nurture and teach her, and when she is married into another’s household as a daughter-in-law her dull-witted husband is unable to serve as a model she can learn from, then she comes to feel that the evil habits of perversity, lewdness, and jealousy cannot be suppressed. But if a girl’s parents, from her childhood until she is given in marriage, instruct her and educate her in the principles of filial obedience to her parents-in-law, respect for her husband, and the need to be gentle and compliant, then even if she marries a husband without ability, she will still know how to stand on her own feet and help her husband establish the family estate; and if the husband she marries is a good man worthy of learning from, then all the more can she give full play to the virtue and capability of a worthy wife and good mother. Therefore to educate a daughter is exactly as important as to educate a son. This truth should be made clear to all the world!
Despising and slighting the spirits of one’s ancestors.

After one’s ancestors and parents have died, their yin spirits remain, and these are called the former spirits (xianling). Whenever the funeral rites lack propriety, the mourning period violates the norms, the burial is not carried out promptly, the sacrifices and prayers are not sincere, the grave-sweeping is not diligent, the ancestral hall is not kept clean, or the incense is lit intermittently—these are all ways of slighting the former spirits. Water has its source and a tree has its root; how can a person forget the spirits of those who came before him? If one is remiss in this, then one does not deserve to be called a human being!
Violating the command of those above.

All persons in a lower position who receive commands from those above are under an ‘upper command’: for example, a minister receiving a command from the ruler, a child receiving a command from a parent, or a disciple receiving a command from his teacher. As for these commands from above—the orders, directives, commissions, and summons—if they are contrary to reason and cannot be carried out, one should explain gently and offer remonstrance beforehand, making clear the reason one dares not accept the command. If, on the other hand, they accord with reason and ought to be done, and one still fails to carry them out diligently, there is already fault in that—how much more so in rebelling against them! And the one who rebels against the command of those above is precisely he who will in time become a rebellious minister or a treacherous son.
Doing things that bring no benefit to oneself.

All the affairs of the world turn empty in the blink of an eye. Only the merit and virtue one cultivates oneself, and the good one does to benefit society by promoting what is beneficial and removing what is harmful—these alone can one carry with oneself, life after life and world after world, in boundless enjoyment. These are the things that are truly beneficial. But building great houses, buying good fields, clothing, and carriages, and collecting every kind of poem, painting, and antique—these are all profitless undertakings, and moreover they can ruin one’s resolve and burden one’s body, with not the slightest benefit. As for hanging lanterns and draping festoons, singing and dancing and performing plays, drinking wine and smoking, gambling and visiting prostitutes—these not only bring no benefit but also do great harm!
Harboring false intentions in secret.

A minister deceiving his ruler, a child rebelling against his parents, a wife betraying her husband, brothers harming one another, and friends overthrowing one another—all these conduct arise from harboring false intentions in secret. Yet harboring false intentions does not need to wait until it is manifested in deed; the moment such a thought stirs, though others may not know it, the ghosts and spirits have already condemned his heart.
Cursing oneself, and also cursing others.

This sentence refers to one who curses without any just cause to plead. Whenever one is angry and resentful beyond bearing, curses oneself to die, and curses others to die too—this is the first sign of disaster befalling the petty man or the woman. It often happens that before one’s time to die has come, one dies at once just as one had cursed, and so how can one be anything but cautious?
Having one’s likes and dislikes perverted by partiality.

The scope of partial dislike or partial affection is wide. Whenever it is a ruler toward his minister, a father toward his son, a husband toward his wife and concubines, or a master toward his servants, this is often present. But for a woman toward the children born of the former wife and the children she herself bore, the case of partial dislike and partial affection is especially severe. Therefore, in ancient times, Master Zeng, after his wife died, never remarried for the rest of his life. Zengzi said: “Yin Gaozong, because of his later wife, killed his own son Xiaoji; the Zhou minister Yin Jifu, also because of a later wife, killed his own son Boqi. I am not the equal of Gaozong, nor of Jifu—how could I be sure not to commit the same error as they?” Excellent! Excellent! Zengzi spoke most truly. Zengzi, fearing that he himself might fall into the fault of partial dislike and partial affection, was the best model of one who could preserve the grace of a father. Yet after his wife had passed away never to remarry—this too is a thing hard for human feeling to achieve. We can only ask that one who remarries constantly bear in mind Zengzi’s words, and perhaps he may not, through partial dislike and affection, commit a great error.
Stepping over wells and stoves.

The benefit of a well to mankind is very great, and there is a spirit of the spring that presides over it, called Guan, whose form is like that of a beautiful woman; moreover the water of the well can supply men and animals, birds and beasts, and can too be used to sacrifice to the gods and make offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—how can one profane and slight it? And among the spirits of the five kinds of sacrifice, the hearth god is one of them; he is the Fire Spirit of Great Unity, surnamed Zhang, named Zhuo, styled Ziguo. He is in charge of the fortune and misfortune of a whole household, and exclusively examines good and evil, knows beforehand auspiciousness and calamity. If one steps over the well or the stove, one slights and insults the spirits, and the offense is very great. And it is not only stepping over them: for example, sitting on the well’s rim, trampling the stove door with one’s foot, or baking filthy things upon the stove—all these are acts that offend and defile the spirits!
Leaping over food and over people’s bodies.

Food is the provision that sustains life, and man is one of the Three Powers, standing alongside Heaven and Earth as the Three Powers (for it is because man can aid Heaven and Earth in transforming and nourishing all things that he stands with them as one of the Three Powers). Therefore to leap over food and to leap over a person’s body are both offenses.
Harming an already-born child and aborting a child still in the womb.

The human body is supremely precious; to obtain a human body is exceedingly difficult. Moreover, at the time a person is born, the heavenly spirits rejoice and the god in charge of destiny settles his reckoning; it can be said to startle heaven and move earth, and its preciousness is beyond description! And when a child is just born, what has it done to owe anything to its parents? Yet some hard-hearted parents dare to kill the infant. Then there is the woman who elopes in lewdness, and after conceiving aborts the child; such conduct is worse than that of birds and beasts, and cannot be guided or made to understand. As for those who, because the family is poor and dislike having too many children, drown the child at birth or abort it before it is born—know that the offense of killing a person is beyond expiation. Even the smallest creature’s life is so precious that one should wish to spare it and avoid killing it—how much more one’s own child! Whenever in this life a person has no child, or raises a child only to have it die, or in old age has the child die before him—these are all fruits born of such evil karma committed in past lives.

When Qian Bangwei served as magistrate of Guixi county, because the local custom was that when a daughter was born many were unwilling to raise her and drowned the infant girls, Qian Bangwei employed both kindness and severity—heavy rewards and heavy punishments—to strictly forbid the drowning of infant girls. If one killed an infant girl, five households were held jointly guilty and punished, and in this way he saved the lives of many baby girls. Qian Bangwei was later promoted to be prefect of Tingzhou, enjoyed a long life, and his descendants all prospered.

Just because he prohibited the people from harming children and aborting the unborn, he was able to obtain such blessings. Today people should at all times counsel others not to commit this evil deed, and the merit too is not small!

Once there was Guo Yin’s daughter, Guo Yinfeng, whose soul was seized by two ghosts and taken through all eighteen hells. She saw that in the last hell there was a King of the Underworld seated in the hall, and beneath the hall several hundred women stood drawn up in order; and each of them had children embracing their feet, weeping and crying: “Give me back my life! Give me back my life!” Some of these women, because they had borne too many daughters, had drowned the infant girls; some were so poor they had raised children and then killed them; some were wives who, jealous of a concubine’s pregnancy, beat the child from her womb; some had conceived an illicit child and then poisoned it; some, through quarrels and fighting, had disturbed the fetal energy and caused a miscarriage; some, disliking the child’s crying, beat or threw the child until it died; and some, being careless and unguarded in caring for the child, brought it to an untimely death. The King of the Underworld questioned each of them one by one. Every woman’s body was bound with chains, her face gaunt and her body thin, looking utterly pitiable. After Guo Yinfeng returned to the living world, she told her father all she had seen. Guo Yin wrote this matter upon the wall of Tianning Temple to warn the world.

The woman Yang Asheng had been poor and sickly from childhood, and in her later years was even more destitute. At the moment of her death she said to herself: “In a former life I was a physician. When I attended the sick I did not examine the illness carefully. On one occasion a woman said there was a poisonous worm in her belly; I could not tell that she was already with child, and at once gave her wine infused with Daphne genkwa, to drive out the worm. As a result the woman died together with the twins in her belly. Because I misdiagnosed the illness and gave the wrong medicine, I killed three lives. The underworld officials punished me for this crime of killing; when I had endured my suffering in the underworld, I was condemned to be reborn as a woman, and this is already the third time in this life; and in life after life I must be a lowly slave, forever enduring the torment of poverty and hunger and thirst, with scarcely a single day of peace. My plight may be told to the physicians of the world, that they take me as a warning!” When she had spoken, Yang Asheng died.

The Emperor Lord Wenchang said: “Children who are not filial to their parents will naturally be punished and executed by the laws of Heaven. But children who are without fault, and are yet killed by their parents—this is the same as killing the people of the world! And when parents wish to kill their children, why do they not restrain their desires? How can they dare to kill people without regard for the principles of Heaven? In this present age, how can one guarantee there are no such persons? I look upon those suffering punishment in the ghost city of Fengdu, and many of them have committed this very offense! Therefore I hope the people of the world will reflect and awaken quickly, and not bring Heaven’s chastisement upon themselves all the sooner!”
Conduct that is largely dark and unrighteous.

Conduct that is hidden and perverse—such things as adultery, robbery, and lewdness—whatever cannot be told to Heaven or spoken before another, all of it is included. Yet among these, the greater ones must surely be the matter of lewdness. Therefore the Most High writes ‘conduct that is largely hidden and perverse’ immediately after ‘harming children and aborting the unborn’—and there is reason for it.

Master Mao Qizong of the Ming said: “North of Fuliang there was a man named Zhang Mingsan, who accompanied his father, who had been transferred to an office, to Qiongya in exile. The official residence they occupied was next door to that of Commander Li. Commander Li’s two daughters were very beautiful, and Zhang Mingsan secretly carried on an affair with them. Later, when Mingsan wanted to return to his old home in Fuliang, he secretly eloped with Commander Li’s two daughters, hiding them first in a boat. Just as they were about to cross the sea, Commander Li rode up in hot pursuit. Mingsan, at his wit’s end, quickly pushed the two sisters into the water and drowned them. Ten years later Mingsan fell ill with a pain in his waist and hired the physician Sun to treat him. After taking the medicine Sun prescribed, the pain in his waist somewhat eased. That night Sun dreamed that he was catching fish on the beach near Limei when suddenly two women, naked, came out of the water toward him and seized his clothing, saying: ‘We two sisters are from Hainan, and have come here especially to treat Zhang Mingsan’s illness. Are you trying to seize our merit?’ And with that they pulled Sun the physician into the water. Sun woke with a start, drenched in a cold sweat. The next morning Sun told Mingsan of his dream, and Mingsan beat his breast and sighed: ‘Alas! My offense has already come before me—is my death near?’ And indeed, after a month or so, Zhang Mingsan died.”

This is a case of conduct darkly hidden between a man and a woman, and of each receiving retribution! Zhang Mingsan and the two sisters first met in secret, and then fled together in secret; yet the two sisters came to die at Zhang Mingsan’s hand, and ten years later Mingsan died at the hands of the two sisters’ vengeful ghosts. One could say the retribution was wonderfully exact and never the slightest bit off. In general, to commit adultery with another’s wife or daughter, and to harm another’s career and reputation—these two matters are the most hidden and perverse of all, and the most wounding to the heart and to the principles of Heaven. Therefore, he who commits adultery with another’s wife or daughter will surely have his own wife or daughter commit adultery with another; and he who harms the career of another will surely have his own career harmed by another. As the saying goes: “In a dark room, if one does something to wrong one’s conscience, the eyes of the spirits see as clearly as lightning!” And so how can one do evil?
Singing, dancing, and performing plays on the days of obscuration (hui) and the winter sacrifices (la).

Hui is the last day of each lunar month, the day on which the hearth god in charge of destiny makes his report of the world’s merit and faults to Heaven. La has five observances, the days on which the heavenly spirits assess the good and evil, offense and blessing, honors and rank, allotted years, and the auspicious and inauspicious, the life and death of people. The first day of the first month is Heaven’s La; the fifth day of the fifth month is Earth’s La; the seventh day of the seventh month is called the La of Virtue; the first day of the tenth month is the Year’s La; and the eighth day of the twelfth month is the La of Princes and Kings. Whenever these days come, if one should have a fault and it be recorded in the black register of the heavenly spirits, it is very hard to redeem it! Moreover, the Northern Emperor of Fengdu and the Great Lord of the Moon bring out, on these very days, the distant ancestors, parents, and kindred of the living, together with the ghosts of the prison-realms, and question them about the length of their time in the underworld, what offense brought them there to suffer, and in what place their graves now lie; and what are the names of their descendants. Having obtained the names and surnames of the descendants, brothers, kindred, and nine generations, they then begin to assemble and verify, to make up the record of offenses of the living descendants. If, from the distant ages, the living descendants have not yet offered rites of release, then the living descendants are sure to be implicated. Moreover, on these days the yin spirits of the ancestors and kindred are all released, each returning to his own home to receive the sacrifices of his descendants. And as descendants, one ought of course to rely upon the power of the Dharma to sacrifice to the former spirits, to redeem the offenses the forebears committed in the past. If instead one carelessly sings and dances, one offends Heaven and Earth, the ancestors, and one’s kindred! Therefore, on the days of hui and la, should one be making offerings for the ancestors, or should one be singing and dancing?

Master Yu Yubi said: “People should on the days of hui and la weigh the merit they have accumulated in daily life, examine and reflect upon themselves, and rouse themselves to reform and advance.” Therefore the Patriarch often urged people, saying: “If one does not first make a round of preparation, when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, you may be sure you will meet with a fine commotion” (that is, at the moment of death one will be all in a flurry). And again he said: “Each of you, try examining yourselves: from childhood to old age, from birth to death, your mind has been fused into one mass with the five desires, the six dusts, afflictions, and karmic consciousness—what, in the end, will be the result? And what is that one turn that is true turning back?” (that is, have you ever reflected and examined yourselves?) “In a sudden instant, breathing stops, the eyes are shut, and this wandering soul after death must follow the good and evil karma made in a lifetime to receive its retribution! Playing such a part, one has gone for nothing through the world of men—this is what is called living in vain and dying in turbulence!” In the ritual of Master Yunqi Lianchi warning the aged, on the last day of each lunar month people are reminded: “Human life is impermanent, swifter even than the breath! Like a fish in a boiling pot, soon to be cooked until it is burnt and rotten; like a lamp before the wind, to be blown out in an instant. Moreover this body must not long from now pass to death, and the road ahead is a blank mist—who knows where one goes? How can one not suddenly reflect and awaken to the impermanence of life? Therefore one must be watchful and cautious, alert and striving, casting down all conditions and fixing the mind on Buddha-recitation!” The Patriarch exhorted and warned everyone with such bitter words and such a compassionate heart—how can we still go singing and dancing on the days of hui and la?

Qiang Fu of Huaiyin was always most careful in guarding his conduct throughout his life, and in dealing with people he was very humble and gentle. Every morning of the first, fifteenth, and la days he recited Buddhist scriptures, bowed to Heaven and Earth and the spirits, never once skipping it. One time, on the dawn of the New Year’s Day, the Heaven’s La, a petty man came drunk and cursed Qiang Fu. Qiang Fu simply shut his door and paid him no heed. His family and neighbors could hardly contain themselves, but Qiang Fu said: “On a fine festival such as this, who is it that does not drink? And when a man is drunk and raves, it is only human nature. If I contended with him, would it not only show how narrow my own heart is?” These words of Qiang Fu touched the heavenly spirits. That evening, as he was dozing, he dreamed he had come to a place where he saw a man wearing a golden crown and a purple robe, who said to him: “Though you endured, on the dawn of the Heaven’s La of the first day, an insult that others could not bear; God has therefore commended you and gives you blessings and long life, and your descendants shall enjoy rank for generation after generation.” Just then Qiang Fu was awakened by his family. Later Qiang Fu indeed lived to be over eighty, and his two sons and one grandson were all recommended to office as tribute students; and his great-grandsons and great-great-grandsons were all scholars of fine repute in the world of education.
The case of Qiang Fu is an example of the retribution of reflecting on oneself on the days of hui and la. If one instead, on these days, wildly shouts and sings,

dances, indulges in wine, and is given over to wanton conduct—since one has already violated the precepts of Heaven, the mind of self-examination is surely lost as well. Such evil karma is indeed enough to consume one’s blessings and emolument and to cut off one’s allotted years!
On the first day of each month and at the dawn of every day, crying out loudly and cursing angrily.

The deeds of a single month take the first day as their foundation, and the deeds of a single day take the morning as their foundation. At such a time one ought to purify the mind, so as to accord with the Way. If one roars and shouts in anger, then the muddy vapor rises with the liver-fire, and the true energy is scattered with the voice; whereupon a person becomes dim of spirit and muddy of breath, and the thoughts of good all vanish! An old poem says: “All the many afflictions arise from not forbearing; at the moment of encounter, as before a mirror, the wonder lies in brightness. The Buddha’s words seek non-contention, and the Confucian books value non-striving. Here is a fine, happy road—yet few in the world walk it.” The Buddhist scriptures say: “Anger is the root of losing all good dharmas and the cause of falling into the evil paths; one should cast it off quickly and not let it grow!” Therefore crying out and raging gravely afflicts and burdens people. Even in ordinary times one should be careful and cautious—how much more on the first day and in the early morning?

Chen Ying’s wife, nee Zhao, was of a strong and quarrelsome nature. Every time the first day of the month came round her condition grew worse, and those going in and out of her house heard only her voice shouting and cursing without end. Then one day a Daoist came to her home. Zhao said to him: “Why have you come to my house?” The Daoist said: “I have come to sell a miracle pill; once you take my pill you can live to be a hundred.” Zhao was delighted at this, bought the pill, and swallowed it, and at once turned dumb.

In the Han, the Minister of Works Diwu Lun, because his mother was old and could not come to live with him in his official residence, every time the days of hui, la, the new moon, and the full moon came round would think of his mother and often weep in grief; he bowed to Heaven and prayed for his mother’s longevity.

Alas! The gentlemen of old thus grieved for their kin in sympathy with the seasons. Then those who on the days of hui and la sing, dance, shout, and rage—for what reason do they do so? Moreover, what has already been said about making offerings and delivering the ancestors in their distant ages is very detailed—why not make a little reflection upon oneself?
Blowing the nose, spitting phlegm, spitting saliva, and urinating while facing north.

The north is where the Lord of the Big Dipper dwells, and the North Pole is the pivot of Heaven; the three realms, the ten directions, and the ten thousand spirits all belong to the North Pole, and so the Dipper of the Midmost Heaven is called Supreme. How then can one defile the place where this honored one resides? According to the rules of propriety, a son or daughter-in-law may not, beside father and mother or parents-in-law, vomit, sneeze, spit, or blow the nose, for to do so is disrespect! Since this is so, to blow the nose or spit against the north, the direction of the spirits, is not permitted—how much more to urinate?

In the state of Wu of old, there was a man who, waking in the night pressed by thirst, rose and went outside the door, and naked, urinated toward the north. He suddenly saw the whole sky filled with black banners and beheld the True Warrior appearing in his form. Startled, he crawled from outside back into his room, lay down on his bed, and was ill for several months; only after repenting did the illness mend.

The ‘Scripture of Long Life’ says: “Spring is the east, summer the south, autumn the west, and winter the north; these are the directions pointed to by the monthly orders, the directions in which the handle of the Big Dipper turns, and they are all offenses against the handle of the Dipper; and by them the shortening of life is most swift.” Looking again at the case above, one comes to know that there are precepts for every direction, and not only for the exact north.

The Qian family of Changshu county in Jiangsu was a great clan of the region. In the Zhengde era of the Ming, the family’s houses caught fire and burned for three days and three nights before going out. Yet in the midst of the ashes of the row upon row of burned buildings, only a small three-story tower was not burned. It was the tower where the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law of the fourth branch of the Qians, both widows, lived. When the flames came pressing in on all four sides, the two, having nowhere to flee, and since they had always reverently worshipped the Dipper Spirit, could only kneel and knock their heads and pray to the Dipper with all their might. Suddenly they saw seven persons in red standing beneath the eaves, who raised their sleeves and waved the fire away, and the fire at once scattered. Thereupon the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law were safe and unharmed. The houses all around were burned to the last stick of timber. The miracle of the two women’s prayer to the Big Dipper affecting their safety moved the people of the region, who all devoutly served the Big Dipper.

All who revere the Big Dipper obtain blessings of lengthened life, removal of illness, preservation of life, escape from disaster, bestowal of happiness, and continuation of descendants; and the examples of the floods, fires, robbers, demons, ghosts, and pestilences that do not harm them are beyond counting. Since one understands this much, how could one blow the nose, spit, or urinate facing north?
Singing and weeping before the stove.

The Yellow Emperor’s ‘Scripture of the Stove’ says: “At the place of the stove one may not sing, intone poems, weep, curse, rage, or shout.” And intoning and weeping, though grief and joy differ, are both acts that slight the spirits, and surely will cut off one’s emoluments and longevity. Now people today, before the authorities, do not dare to speak loudly or tell lies—why then do they dare behave recklessly before the spirits? These are things that every person ought earnestly to refrain from! As for the blessings and calamities of reverence and profanity, these have already been explained in detail earlier.
Again, lighting incense with the fire of the stove.

According to the ordinances of the school of the Heavenly Master: “The gray fire beneath the stove is called the secret dung of the crouching dragon.” Therefore one may not use the fire of the stove to light incense. And the taboos of incense and fire spoken of in the religious canons are not confined to this one matter alone. For example, using a paper spill soiled and stained by grease as tinder to burn paper money—this is called vainly piling up wax money; such vainly burned wax money piles up at Mount Tai as high as a mountain, and the assemblies of Heaven and Earth, yin and yang, are all unwilling to accept it. Again, in offering to the True Warrior: in summer one may not offer plums, and in winter one may not offer pomegranates; and in inviting the supreme truths to descend, one may not burn nipple-wood incense. Moreover sandalwood is called bath incense, the rose is called the out-of-season flower, and the tung-flower is called the ghost flower—all of these should be avoided. Rather than offend by not avoiding them and bring guilt upon oneself, why not reverently observe the rules of the teaching?

The ‘Collection of the Essentials of the Sutras’ says: “Because there are forms, one may awaken to principle; therefore one must rely upon forms to draw one into the true meaning. So one gazes upon the holy countenance, and relies upon flowers and incense in making offerings.” The Buddha said: “After the Thus-Come-One is extinguished, if a man can use a single flower or a single incense to make offering to the Three Jewels, use one handful of pure water to cleanse the offerings, and with a reverent heart come before the Buddha and call the name of Namo Buddha once—that man falling into the three evil paths is an impossibility.” The ‘Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sutra’ says: “Incense is the name for turning away from filth, and it has the function of spreading fragrance, scattering its perfume, and lifting its fragrance aloft.” The ‘Record of Mystery-Responses’ says: “The foul breath of the human world rises up to Heaven for four hundred thousand li; and the heavens being pure, none of them but loathes the foul breath of the human world. Yet because they have received the Buddha’s entrustment, and the Buddha commanded the heavenly spirits to protect the Dharma, and the Buddha himself still lived among men, therefore the heavenly spirits dare not but come to the human world. Thus in the Dharma of the Buddha, incense may well be called the foremost in Buddhist worship.” The ‘Avataṃsaka Sutra’ says: “In the Good-Dharma Hall of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three there is an incense called pure and majestic; if one burns a single ball of the pure and majestic incense, its fragrance pervades all the heavens, causing the heavenly spirits to think of the Buddha and to attain the Buddha-recitation samadhi.” This being so—can lighting incense with the fire of the stove really go unadmonished?

In the Song, Zhou Kaishan could recite the ‘Avataṃsaka Sutra,’ and there was another monk who could recite the ‘Diamond Sutra.’ The two suddenly died at the same time. The King of the Underworld asked Kaishan to recite the ‘Avataṃsaka Sutra’ and treated him with great reverence; and asked the other monk to recite the ‘Diamond Sutra,’ and his heart was not so reverent. After they had finished, the King said: “You two, because of the merit of reciting the sutras, have both had your lives extended by twenty-four years; but Kaishan, who holds the ‘Avataṃsaka,’ is to be the more highly regarded; and he will not be coming to the underworld again.” At this, the monk who recited the ‘Diamond Sutra’ was deeply ashamed, and asked where Kaishan dwelt, desiring to go visit him. When he awoke, the monk went directly to Luzhou to visit Kaishan and ask him the reason. Kaishan said: “Whenever I recite the sutra, I first put on clean clothes, sprinkle and sweep the room with perfumed water, and then use stones to strike fire or drill wood to draw fire to light the incense. When making the offering, I first revere my own mind, and when I open my mouth to recite, I am as reverent as if I stood before the true Buddha, never daring to be careless or slight. If there be no purification of fire, I absolutely dare not use any other fire to light the incense.” The monk who recited the ‘Diamond Sutra’ thanked him, saying: “I have sinned! Whenever I recited, I often used the fire of the stove to light the incense. For this alone my disrespect is far too great!”
